Long-term management of asthma requires control of inflammation, as well as identification and avoidance of triggers. C
Chronic asthma is treated on the basis of disease severity (see ). An inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) should be included in the long-term treatment for most patients. A
Long-acting beta agonists (LABAs) are the preferred add-on agent for patients taking an inhaled corticosteroid, but they should not be used as monotherapy. A

background.definition: Asthma is a chronic lower respiratory disease characterized by chronic airway inflammation associated with reversible airflow obstruction and airway hyperresponsiveness. The disorder results from an interaction between genetic and environmental factors. In susceptible individuals, typical symptoms include recurrent episodes of coughing, wheezing, breathlessness, and chest tightness. Asthmatic episodes are usually associated with widespread but variable airflow obstruction that is often reversible either spontaneously or with treatment.

list.listitem: 7.5% of US children.
7.7% of US adults.
Over $50 billion per year in the United States.
Asthma accounts for 9.8 million physician office visits per year.
Acute exacerbations of asthma account for 1.8 million emergency department visits per year.
There are approximately 190,000 hospital admissions per year with asthma as the primary diagnosis.
Asthma results from an interaction between genetics and environmental factors.

Early exposure to house-dust mite and cockroach antigens is associated with the development of asthma. Respiratory infections during childhood, particularly respiratory syncytial virus and parainfluenza virus, can also contribute.

Nonrespiratory infections at young ages may protect against the development of asthma by modulating expression of T helper type 2 cytokines. This is termed as the hygiene hypothesis. A study comparing Hutterite and Amish children found more asthma and higher eosinophil levels in Hutterite children, where farming is mechanized and presumably cleaner.

Exposure to light at night (i.e. artificial light at night, evening chronotype, and night shift work) is associated with increased likelihood of having allergic diseases including asthma. This association is stronger in youths than in adults.
The precise identification of genetic predisposition remains under investigation. Current data show that multiple genes may be involved and vary in different ethnic groups.
Acute and chronic inflammation is the key driver of asthma.
Reversible airway obstruction is caused by airway hyperresponsiveness, bronchoconstriction, and airway edema.
Some obstruction may be irreversible due to airway remodeling; it is unclear how treatment influences this process.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Antibiotic use in first year of life
Note: Risk is for current diagnosis of asthma, not current wheeze or bronchial hyperresponsiveness.

list.listitem: Screening for asthma is not generally recommended. Clinicians should be alert to the possibility of asthma in patients with episodic symptoms, especially when occuring after allergen exposure; seasonal variability of symptoms; atopy and family history of asthma. C

One cohort study of 806 mother-offspring pairs found an association between vitamin D insufficiency during pregnacy and later asthma in offspring, though a randomized trial found no benefit to vitamin D supplementation. B

Fish oil supplementation in pregnant mothers may be effective at decreasing the risk of their offspring developing asthma. A Danish study randomized 695 pregnant women to long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (fish oil) or placebo. They found that it reduced the likelihood of wheezing disorders among their offspring (16.9% vs 23.7%, NNT = 14). A subsequent meta-analysis of 10 RCTs which included a total of 3,676 infants suggested on sub-group analysis that while maternal fish oil supplementation did significantly reduce the risk of asthma, it did not reduce the risk of wheeze. High-dose supplementation seemed to have a stronger effect. B

A population-based case-finding study to identify patients with undiagnosed asthma or COPD called 1.2 million Canadians, identified 49,594 who answered the phone and said that someone in the household had respiratory symptoms, of whom 4272 potentially had undiagnosed asthma or COPD, of whom 595 were found to have airflow obstruction and were given a diagnosis of asthma or COPD. Patients randomized to intensive guideline directed therapy by specialists had no difference in ED visits, hospitalizations, or a clinically meaningful change in symptoms (3.5 points on a 100 point scale) compared to those managed as usual by primary care doctors.
Spirometry should be obtained in all patients with suspected asthma. C
At least partial reversibility of airflow obstruction on spirometry following beta 2 agonist administration is a hallmark of asthma. C
Bronchoprovocative challenge testing with methacholine is a sensitive test that can be used when the diagnosis of asthma is in question. C

list.listitem: Typical symptoms include recurrent dyspnea, wheezing, cough (particularly nocturnal or chronic), and/or chest tightness. Patients often note worsening symptoms following exposure to cold, animals, exercise, viral infection, smoke, pollen, or menstrual cycles.

A study of 290 Finnish university students found that cough with wheeze distinct from a respiratory tract infection and episodes of shortness of breath associated with wheeze were the strongest predictors of an asthma diagnosis.
Suggestive physical findings include expiratory wheeze, upper airway edema, eczema, and decreased peak expiratory flow.

In children, a parent- or patient-provided history of noisy breathing, chest pain, or breathing problems is most strongly associated with an increased risk of diagnosis of asthma, especially when present with cough.
May have personal or family history of ezcema and/or allergic rhinitis as part of the atopic triad.

One study of 32 patients found that African-American subjects used upper airway words to describe their symptoms: "tight throat"; "voice tight"; "itchy throat"; "tough breath"; and "scared-agitated" were the general types of descriptors used. White subjects used lower airway words to describe their symptoms: "need to take a deep breath"; "out of air"; "aware of breathing"; "hurts to breathe"; and "lightheaded". None of the African-American subjects used either "shortness of breath" or "wheezing" to describe their symptoms, and only one white subject did.

Spirometry is the key diagnostic test for asthma. A decreased forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity ratio (FEV1/FVC ratio) is suggestive of obstructive lung disease. However, asthma is an intermittent disease, and normal spirometry does not exclude the diagnosis.

Bronchodilator response to a short-acting bronchodilator (such as albuterol) during spirometry defines reversible airway obstruction, a hallmark of asthma. Significant reversibility is defined as improvement of 12% or more in baseline FEV1 or 10% improvement of percent predicted FEV1.

Provocative methacholine challenge testing is the most sensitive test to confirm a diagnosis of asthma when the clinical diagnosis is not clear. A positive result is defined as a decrease in FEV1 by more than 20% at 8 mg/mL. The test is sensitive with a high negative predictive value to rule out asthma.

Measurements of fractional exhaled nitrous oxide and the sputum eosinophil count are emerging tests that are not yet well standardized. However, there is some evidence that using them to monitor adult patients with asthma reduces the frequency of exacerbations and hospitalizations.
Peak flow meters are designed to monitor, not diagnose, asthma. There is no difference in peak flow measurements between standing and seated healthy adults.

While chest x-rays, serological tests, and allergy testing may be used in the diagnostic workup and may have features consistent with asthma, e.g. eosinophilia on a CBC differential, they are not appropriate tools to diagnose asthma.
Models have been developed to predict hospital admission for children during an acute exacerbation, as well as prediction of asthma relapse in adults after an acute exacerbation.
A validated risk score can predict the likelihood that a child age 1 to 3 years will be diagnosed with asthma in the next 5 years.

A study performed at Cleveland Clinic analyzing outpatient electronic health record data of over 60,000 patients showed that models built with a machine learning algorithm accurately predicted asthma exacerbation.

Important criteria to establish a diagnosis of asthma include episodic symptoms of airflow obstruction or airway hyperresponsiveness, airflow obstruction that is at least partially reversible, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses.

Establishing a diagnosis is important for initiating appropriate treatment. This leads to reduced asthma symptoms, a decreased requirement of rescue medications, optimization of lung function, and a reduction of future asthma exacerbations.

Spirometry may be helpful in diagnosing asthma, but there is no evidence clearly demonstrating improved patient-oriented outcomes with regular monitoring. Of note, home- vs. office-based spirometry readings may not be interchangeable, with home spirometry having disagreement with and less consistency than clinic spirometry (at least for the devices and coaching modalities used in the CAPTAIN and 205832 trials).
Patients should be assessed and educated on use of proper technique for inhaled medications and environmental triggers. C
In general, all patients with persistent asthma require at least one controller medication containing an ICS. A
Single maintenance and reliever therapy (SMART) with ICS-formoterol is the preferred treatment for moderate to severe persistent asthma in patients ages 4 years and older. A
All patients should have as-needed inhaler therapy prescribed. Appropriate medications are either SABA or ICS-formoterol, depending on the asthma severity. A
Leukotriene receptor antagonists are acceptable controller agents, but are less effective as monotherapy compared with inhaled corticosteroids in mild persistent asthma. A
Monoclonal antibodies such as omalizumab and dupilumab provide a small reduction in exacerbations for patients with poorly-controlled asthma, but are costly.B

Drug therapy is guided by disease severity (see ) placing patients into Step 1 (mild intermittent asthma) or Steps 2-6 (mild to severe persistent asthma). A stepwise approach to drug therapy is recommended to gain and maintain control of asthma (see ). This is based on NHLBI National Asthma Education and Prevention Program guidelines.

Evidence of treatment efficacy is based on reduction in exacerbations, improvement in lung function, and improved quality of life. The goal of treatment is to achieve and maintain control, which is demonstrated by tolerating normal daily activities, daytime symptoms occurring less than 2 days per week, and symptomatic nighttime awakenings occurring less than once per month.
Patients with more than two exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids should be treated as having persistent asthma, regardless of symptoms.

It is important to closely monitor symptoms, response to treatment, and even the need for therapy at all. In a study of adults with physician-diagnosed asthma, 701 patients with mild to moderate asthma underwent spirometry and serial bronchial challenge testing. Those not confirmed to have asthma based on that testing had their medication tapered over four visits, and were followed for a year. Overall, about a third of patients had a current diagnosis of asthma ruled out.

When implementing step-down therapy, consider reducing corticosteroid dose and/or shifting from oral to inhaled steroids; adding a leukotriene antagonist to lower the steroid dose; and using allergen immunotherapy.

When initiating corticosteroids, a moderate starting dose is preferred based on the conclusions of a Cochrane review of 26 randomized trials. Starting with a high dose and then stepping down as tolerated offered no long-term advantages.

A systematic review comparing different doses of inhaled corticosteroids found some benefit for high-dose over moderate-dose, but it was only clinically significant for patients at higher risk of severe exacerbation. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent a severe exacerbation was 19 if the patient's baseline risk was 50%, 28 if it was 20%, and 91 if it was 5%.

For mild intermittent asthma, the 2020 NHLBI guidelines recommend monotherapy with an as-needed SABA for patients age 12 and older. On the other hand, the 2022 Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) guidelines recommends an as-needed low dose ICS-formoterol or low dose ICS used whenever a SABA is used as reliever therapy because short-acting medications alone increase the risk of severe exacerbations and death. It is worth noting that many of the GINA authors report potential conflicts of interest related to involvement with pharmaceutical companies.

The most recent NHLBI guidelines recommend that patients ages 12 years and older with mild persistent asthma use either an as-needed SABA with a daily low dose ICS, or else concomitant use of an ICS and SABA on an as-needed basis.

For those with mild-to-moderate persistent asthma, a systematic review of eight RCTs with 1,669 participants found no benefit to increasing the dose of an ICS during an exacerbation in patients with mild-to-moderate asthma.This is in line with the most recent 2020 NHLBI guidelines, which generally do not recommend temporarily increasing the ICS dose for an increase in asthma symptoms. Notably, a large RCT with 1,922 patients showed that clinically significant exacerbations were reduced by temporarily quadrupling an inhaled corticosteroid dose when asthma symptoms flared (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.71-0.92, p = 0.002).

A trial randomized 2516 persons 12 and older with poorly controlled mild asthma to as needed albuterol 90 mcg + budesonide 160 mcg or albuterol alone. Patients could take up to 6 doses (12 puffs) in a 24-hour period. After approximately one year of follow-up, the albuterol-budesonide rescue inhaler group had fewer severe exacerbations in the ITT analysis (5.3% vs 9.4%; P < .001, number needed to treat = 26).

The 2020 NHLBI update suggests that in children up to four years of age who only experience wheezing with respiratory infections, a seven- to 10-day course of ICS daily at the start of a respiratory infection reduces exacerbations and systemic corticosteroid use. The effects of short-term ICS use on growth are uncertain, but they are likely less than systemic corticosteroids.

A Cochrane review concluded that a single inhaler with budesonide-formoterol (steroid + LABA) reduced exacerbations requiring an oral corticosteroid (NNT = 14); the comparison was usually an inhaled corticosteroid alone. A combined analysis of four 26-week RCTs concluded that adding a LABA to an inhaled corticosteroid reduced non-severe asthma exacerbations (NNT = 53 over 6 months) but not severe exacerbations (0.60% for ICS vs 0.66% for ICS + LABA).

An RCT of 668 patients showed that as-needed budesonide-formoterol reduced the risk of severe exacerbations when compared to SABA given as-needed, and was as effective at preventing exacerbations as maintenance budesonide plus SABA given as-needed (0.195/year and 0.175/year respectively, NNT = 5 to prevent 1 exacerbation over 1 year).

An RCT with 2516 participants with poorly controlled mild asthma (12 and older) randomized them to either 2 puffs of budesonide 80 mcg plus albuterol 90 mcg OR 2 puffs of albuterol 90 mcg alone from a rescue inhaler. Patients could take up to 6 doses (12 puffs) in a 24-hour period. The combination therapy had fewer severe exacerations after one year (5.3% vs 9.4%, p = 0.001, NNT = 26).

Another RCT of 884 adults with asthma who were only using a SABA or a SABA with low-to-moderate doses of ICS randomized them to relief therapy with a SABA+ICS or daily use of ICS plus reliever therapy with a SABA. Those using relief therapy with SABA + ICS and no daily maintenance therapy actually had slightly fewer severe exacerbations.
LABAs should never be used as monotherapy due to increased risk of serious adverse events such as exacerbations and death if not paired with inhaled corticosteroids.

In patients with stable asthma, pre-exercise dosing of short acting beta-agonists were more effective than mast cell stabilizers and anticholinergics at protecting against exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, though all were effective and had few adverse effects.
In children 2 years and younger, salbutamol (albuterol) used as a rescue for wheeze was well tolerated.

In adults, a prospective cohort study found that harms were uncommon in adults using inhaled corticosteroids for one year. Low-dose use is not associated with adverse harms, but medium-dose use is associated with a 2-fold relative increased risk and high-dose use is associated with a 3- to 5-fold increased risk.

In patients four years and older with moderate-to-severe persistent asthma, it is recommended to use single maintenance and reliever therapy (SMART). This involves a combination of an ICS and the long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) formoterol being used both as a daily controller and a rescue inhaler to a maximum of 12 puffs daily for patients older than 12 years. SMART using other LABA medications has not been studied.

Control of severe asthma requires high-dose inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting beta agonist. An RCT of patients with moderate persistent asthma and 1 to 4 exacerbations in the previous year found that adding formoterol to budesonide was safe, and led to a small reduction in exacerbations (NNT = 63). A second study compared fluticasone + salmeterol with fluticasone alone in 11,751 patients with moderate-to-severe asthma and at least one severe exacerbation in the previous year. There were fewer severe exacerbations in the combined treatment group (NNT = 50 over 6 months) and harms were similar between groups.

A Cochrane review with 41 studies involving 27,951 adults and 8 studies involving 8,453 children found the addition of salmeterol to ICS resulted in a non-fatal serious adverse event for 1 in 152 adults and 1 in 139 children over an average of 6 months.

An RCT of 3,132 patients with moderate-to-severe asthma who were taking long-term inhaled corticosteroids randomized them to relief therapy with a rescue inhaler of albuterol 180 mcg-budesonide 160 mcg, albuterol 180 mcg-budesonide 80 mcg or albuterol 180 mcg. Patients in the higher-dose budesonide group had significantly fewer severe exacerbations and reduction in need for systemic corticosteroids compared to the albuterol only group.

In children, when added to an inhaled corticosteroid, LABA therapy is superior in improving lung function compared to the same or higher doses of ICS. However, LABA therapy does not result in a reduction in exacerbations requiring systemic steroids. This was confirmed in a 2016 RCT enrolling 6250 children with frequent exacerbations.

In the most recent NHLBI update for 2020, adding a LABA is recommended instead of adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) in patients with uncontrolled asthma despite daily ICS therapy. Although effects on symptoms are similar, adding a LAMA may be associated with increased harm. Adding a LAMA to an ICS may be indicated if unable to use ICS-LABA medications. Adding a LAMA when ICS-LABA therapy does not adequately control asthma symptoms does not decrease the frequency of exacerbations but is associated with increased asthma control. LAMA medications should be avoided in patients at risk for glaucoma or urinary retention.

Two RCTs compared step-up strategies for black adults and children whose asthma was not controlled by a low-dose ICS. The study revealed that for black children with poorly controlled asthma using an ICS, effective treatment options include increasing the ICS dose or adding salmeterol. In contrast, for black adolescents and adults, the study showed greater treatment efficacy by adding salmeterol and then, if needed, increasing the ICS dose.

The addition of a long-acting beta agonist (LABA) is marginally superior to a leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) in patients not adequately controlled on low dose ICS. Outcomes assessed were exacerbations requiring corticosteroids, lung function and rescue medication use, symptoms and quality-of-life.
Either a leukotriene receptor antagonist, theophylline, or zileuton may be added to high dose inhaled steroids and a long-acting beta 2 agonist in patients with poorly controlled severe asthma.

Long-term oral corticosteroids should be used only in individuals not responding to other medications. A systematic review of chronic corticosteroid use or frequent steroid bursts in asthma identified an increased clinical burden of adverse outcomes including opportunistic infections, gastrointestinal bleeds, osteoporosis, and hypertension as compared to non-oral corticosteroid users.

A large UK registry concluded that one year of ICS use is associated with a low rate of serious adverse events but there is a dose-dependent increased risk with higher doses. Low-dose use is not associated with harms such as MACE, PE, or pneumonia, but medium-dose use is associated with a 2-fold relative increased risk and high-dose use is associated with a 3- to 5-fold increased risk.

A Cochrane review concluded that adding an anticholinergic for patients whose asthma is not well-controlled by standard therapies provides little or no benefit. A subsequent systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 trials with 4,998 patients noted improved lung function but no reduction in adverse events (such as asthma attacks) with the use of tiotropium for patients with moderate-to-severe asthma.

Two parallel, double-blinded, randomized controlled trials assigned adults aged 18-75 with uncontrolled asthma to receive a single triple therapy inhaler including an ICS+LABA+long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) or ICS+LABA for 52 weeks. Primary outcomes included FEV1 at 26 weeks and rate of moderate/severe exacerbations over 52 weeks. Compared to the ICS+LABA group, the triple therapy group experienced an FEV1 improvement of 57 mL (95% CI 15-99; p = 0.0080) in one study and 73 mL (95% CI 26-120; p = 0.0025) in the other. Additionally, moderate and severe exacerbations were modestly reduced by 15% (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.99; p = 0.033) in the first study and 12% (rate ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.75-1.03; p = 0.11) in the other when compared to ICS+LABA group. Analyzed separately, the difference was statistically significant for moderate exacerbations (1.52 vs 1.72 per year) but not for severe exacerbations (0.24 vs 0.31 per year). Having 0.2 fewer is equivalent to an NNT of 5 to prevent one moderate exacerbation per year.

A Cochrane review identified 10 trials with a total of only 185 patients evaluating the effect of methotrexate on reducing steroid use in steroid-dependent asthma patients. There was a small reduction in daily steroid dose (3-4 mg) but given the adverse effects of methotrexate and poor quality of the evidence base, this therapy is not recommended.

Omalizumab should be considered in patients with severe asthma who have a perennial allergic component. Anti-IgE treatment with omalizumab can be effective in reducing asthma exacerbations and hospitalizations as an adjunctive therapy to ICS and during steroid tapering phases for patients older than 12 years with moderate-to-severe asthma.

Once weekly dupilumab (a monoclonal antibody to interleukin-4 receptors that inhibits inflammatory pathways) in poorly-controlled asthma patients with eosinophilia (>300 cells/uL) or elevated sputum eosinophil count (>3%) was not associated with any clinical improvement when added to background therapy of ICS and LABA. A study in patients with moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma randomized them to dupilumab 200 mg to 300 mg every 2 weeks or placebo. The active treatment group experienced approximately 1 fewer severe exacerbation every 2.5 years, but cost of the drug is $35,000 per year.

An RCT found that compared to placebo, in patients with eosinophilic asthma epemokimab reduces asthma exacerbations (NNT = 167) but the impact on severe exacerbations requiring hospitalization or an ED visit is minimal (NNT = 1428).
An RCT of 219 adults with asthma not well-controlled by an ICS randomized them to either lebrikizumab 250 mg subcutaneously once a month or placebo; there was no difference in outcomes.

Benralizumab is a human monoclonal antibody against IL-5 receptors. In a randomized trial of 220 patients with severe asthma, use of the drug (30 mg SC every 4 weeks and then every 8 weeks) reduced the long-term median daily dose of prednisone from 10 to 5 mg. Serious exacerbations were slightly less likely as well (0.2 vs 0.32/year, p = 0.02).

An RCT of 1,061 patients with severe, uncontrolled asthma who received the monoclonal antibody tezepelumab, compared to placebo, experienced fewer exacerbations (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.37-0.53) as well as improved asthma control and quality of life.

In a pair of randomized trials of 762 patients with severe eosinophilic asthma, depemokimab reduced any asthma exacerbations in patients with eosinophilic asthma (NNT = 167) but the impact on severe exacerbations requiring hospitalization or an ED visit was minimal (NNT = 1428). If it costs US$15,000 per year, that would be ($15,000 x 167) $2.5 million to prevent any exacerbation and ($15,000 x 1428) $21.4 million to prevent a serious exacerbation.

A small sample, short duration, open-label, randomized controlled trial showed a dramatic improvement in asthma control and decrease in exacerbations among children with poorly controlled asthma with the use of azithromycin 3 times per week.
A randomized trial showed that azithromycin can prevent severe lower respiratory tract infections in children prone to these infections if used early in the disease process.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies with 855 patients found no benefit of azithromycin over placebo on exacerbation frequency.

A Cochrane review identified 25 studies with 1973 patients with asthma randomizing them to macrolide or placebo. They conclude that macrolides probably deliver a moderately-sized decrease in hospitalizations (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.120-1.12) although this was not statistically significant and is based on only 2 studies with 529 patients. They also found a reduction in ED visits and/or need for systemic corticosteroids (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.53-0.80).

Treatment of gastroesophageal reflux may help in some asthmatics, but there is no reliable way to predict who will benefit. Aggressive treatment with proton pump inhibitors did not help patients with poorly controlled asthma, nor patients with asthma and symptomatic reflux.

Subcutaneous immunotherapy (repeated subcutaneous injections for desensitization) is an option if skin testing or in-vitro antigen-specific immunoglobulin E testing suggests that allergen exposure worsens asthma control. Subcutaneous immunotherapy is not recommended for patients with severe asthma because of risks of complications. In patients with mild or moderate asthma, immunotherapy may improve asthma symptoms. Sublingual immunotherapy is approved for allergic rhinitis but not for asthma. Patients with asthma should not administer immunotherapy at home.
Pneumococcal vaccine may reduce exacerbations.

Influenza vaccine does not induce exacerbations, but its protective effect against exacerbations remains unclear. One retrospective cohort study followed 466 Omani adults with asthma for a year after influenza vaccination and found that those who were vaccinated had a significantly reduced frequency of upper respiratory tract infection (37.9% vs 73%), but no significant reduction in asthma exacerbation frequency.
A Cochrane review concluded that breathing exercises and aerobic exercise can improve symptoms, quality of life, and some measures of lung function.
Patients with stable asthma should be encouraged to participate in regular exercise training without fear of symptom exacerbation.
In a randomized controlled trial of adults (N = 51) with moderate-to-severe asthma, increased physical activity produced improvements in asthma control (ACQ score 95% CI -0.8 [-1.1 to -0.4]).
There is no evidence that fish oil supplementation, dietary sodium,vitamin C, vitamin D,spinal manipulation, and cyclosporine are effective in patients with chronic asthma.
An intensive, year-long intervention to deliver pest management services to the homes of mouse-sensitized and mouse-exposed children and adolescents had no effect on asthma symptoms or exacerbations.

An unblinded trial found that eradication of household mold decreased asthma symptoms and medication use. Similarly, sublingual allergen immunotherapy for house dust mites reduced asthma exacerbations in adults with poorly controlled allergic asthma and allergic rhinitis.

A Cochrane review concluded that there was no evidence to support the use of household air ionizers. Further, there is limited evidence to support the use of speleotherapy (spending extended time in an underground environment) in children with asthma.
Self-management using written action plans based on symptoms and peak flow measurements may improve outcomes, especially in more severe disease.
Guided self-management has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality.

An RCT of 911 patients demonstrated a decrease in hospitalization (6.4% vs 3.3%, NNT = 32) through identifying "high-risk" patients with asthma. A standardized approach was employed to managing such patients after they contacted the office (including prompt appointments, identification of those who did not fill their medications, etc). Patients in the intervention arm were also more likely to receive guideline appropriate care.

A Cochrane review from 2013 found that evidence is insufficient to advise practitioners, patients and policymakers on the efficacy of smartphone apps in the self-management of asthma, though this is being increasingly investigated. A more recent, small (60-patient) RCT found that such an app did lead to significantly improved asthma control and quality of life compared to control patients after 6 months.

Asthma coaching, an intentional intervention aimed at identifying and targeting barriers to self-management as well as longitudinal reinforcement, demonstrated improved quality of life and decreased emergency department visits at 1 year compared to placebo in adults 60 years or older with uncontrolled moderate to severe asthma (OR = 0.8; 95% CI 0.6-0.99). An RCT in Malawi demonstrated similar results for pediatric patients receiving personalized asthma coaching.

In bronchial thermoplasty, radiofrequency energy is delivered by a catheter to bronchi to limit the volume of airway smooth muscle. It is often reserved as a last line treatment option for severe persistent asthma.
See chapter on Asthma (acute exacerbation).

Referral to a specialist should be considered for patients with difficulty in achieving or maintaining control of asthma, after more than two bursts of oral systemic corticosteroids in 1 year, after an exacerbation requiring hospitalization, or if immunotherapy or monoclonal antibody treatments are being considered.
See chapter on Asthma (acute exacerbation).
Inhaled corticosteroid use controls asthma symptoms but does not change the underlying disease process. B
Mild asthma often does not persist into adulthood, and persistent asthma often improves over time. B
A post-bronchodilator peak expiratory flow (PEF) of less than 80% predicted should prompt increased monitoring; less than 50% requires immediate medical evaluation. A

Asthma severity often decreases over time. A study of 188 children found that among 111 meeting criteria for severe asthma, only 30% were still classified as severe 3 years later. Another study that followed school age children in Melbourne with a history or wheezing until the age of 50 found that remission rates of what would now be categorized as intermittent asthma and persistent asthma were 64% and 15%, respectively. In the former group, most remissions occurred prior to age 10.
Adults with asthma may have a decline in lung function over time that is often seen with aging.
Inhaled corticosteroid use controls asthma symptoms but does not change the underlying disease process.
Asthma that occurs after the age of 3 years generally does not impair normal lung growth.
Asthma without concomitant COPD is not associated with increased mortality.

A study group from Denmark has suggested that "clinical remission" may be a reasonable goal in some patients with severe asthma treated with biologics, finding that 97/501 biologic-naive patients treated for 12 months achieved this. They defined clinical remission as no asthma exacerbations, no use of maintenance oral corticosteroids, well-controlled asthma symptoms (ACQ-6 score of ≤ 1.5), and pulmonary function normalization determined by FEV1.

Monitoring should focus on daytime asthma symptoms (e.g., wheezing, cough, chest tightness, or shortness of breath), nocturnal awakening as a result of asthma symptoms, inability or difficulty performing normal activities (including exercise), and frequency of rescue medication use.
An RCT found that spirometry every 3 months was no better than usual care in adults with asthma or COPD.
A post-bronchodilator PEF of less than 80% predicted should prompt increased monitoring, whereas less than 50% indicates an immediate need for medical evaluation.
Patients on high-dose ICS should be monitored for steroid-related side effects.
Inhaled budesonide is often the preferred ICS preparation in pregnancy.
Prostaglandin F2-alpha (carboprost) is contraindicated for termination of pregnancy or treating postpartum bleeding due to risks for bronchoconstriction.

In one analysis of about 650 women with asthma, infants born to mothers that used systemic corticosteroids had a lower birth weight compared to those who were born to mothers who used beta-2 agonists but not systemic corticosteroids. Notably, the rate of infants with SGA (small for gestational age) was not significantly different between the groups. Based on a subsequent linear regression analysis, the authors suggest that the systemic steroids contributed more to this finding than the asthma itself.
Inhaled corticosteroids remain the preferred treatment for all children except those with mild intermittent asthma.

An ATS guideline on the evaluation of wheezing in infants recommends (based on very low or low quality evidence) the following: (1) consider bronchoscopy, alveolar lavage, esophageal pH monitoring and swallowing studies for diagnosis, and (2) do not use empiric trials of food avoidance, upper GI imaging, and radionuclide studies.
Inhaled corticosteroids do not cause clinically significant or irreversible effects on vertical growth, bone mineral density, ocular toxicity, or suppression of adrenal/pituitary axis (see and ).

When added to an inhaled corticosteroid, LABA therapy is superior in improving lung function compared to the same or higher doses of ICS. LABA therapy does not result in a reduction in exacerbations requiring systemic steroids. This was confirmed in a 2016 RCT with 6250 children with frequent exacerbations randomized to fluticasone alone or fluticasone + salmeterol, which found no reduction in severe exacerbations or hospitalizations.

In children with recurrent wheezing associated respiratory illness, early azithromycin (especially in those with frequent episodes) reduces the number of severe infections. In the study, azithromycin was administered in a dose of 12 mg/kg once daily for 5 days as soon as the parents noted signs or symptoms of a respiratory infection.
In children with mild persistent asthma, a randomized trial with 300 children did not find any increase in exacerbations in children randomized to acetaminophen.

An RCT involving 168 parents of children ages 3 to 12 found that 4 weeks of group Acceptance and Commitment Therapy significantly reduced emergency department visits (6-month incident rate ratio 0.20, CI 0.08-0.53, p = 0.003) in comparison with asthma education.

A meta-analysis of 15 longitudinal studies (of low-to-moderate quality) found that asthma education programs in children reduced the risk of hospitalization, ED visits, and office visits. Another study found school-based self-management reduced emergency department visits and hospitalizations among children ages 5 to 18.
